content: The Baby-friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) offers detailed guidance on the implementation, training, monitoring, assessment, and re-assessment of the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding. It also incorporates the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, which was adopted by the 34th World Health Assembly (WHA) in 1981. This code provides recommendations to regulate the marketing of breast-milk substitutes, feeding bottles, and teats. Subsequent WHA resolutions have further supported these efforts. The BFHI has been shown to improve breastfeeding outcomes, with a dose-response relationship observed between the number of interventions a mother is exposed to and the likelihood of improved breastfeeding outcomes. This guideline examines each practice within the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding, consolidating evidence and considerations to inform clinical practice. The scope of the guideline is limited to specific practices that can be implemented in facilities providing maternity and newborn services, aiming to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding. It does not aim to be a comprehensive guide for all potential breastfeeding interventions, such as community-based practices, peer support, or workplace breastfeeding support. Additionally, it does not review the articles and provisions of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes or its related WHA resolutions. The guideline complements other interventions presented in resources such as the Essential Newborn Care Course, Kangaroo Mother Care: A Practical Guide, and the Standards for Improving Quality of Maternal and Newborn Care in Health Facilities. It does not replace these resources but serves as an additional tool. An implementation guide encompassing the recommendations in this guideline, the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, and the BFHI has been developed by WHO and UNICEF and will be published separately. The purpose of this guideline is to provide global, evidence-informed recommendations on protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities that provide maternity and newborn services. This is intended as a public health intervention to optimize breastfeeding practices and improve nutrition, health, and developmental outcomes. The recommendations are targeted at policymakers, expert advisers, technical staff, and program managers involved in designing and scaling up infant and young child feeding programs. Healthcare professionals, clinicians, universities, and training institutions may also use this guideline to disseminate information. The guideline is relevant to women delivering in hospitals, maternity facilities, or other facilities providing maternity and newborn services, as well as their infants. This includes mother-infant pairs with term infants, preterm infants, low-birth-weight infants, sick infants, and those admitted to neonatal intensive care units. Additional guidance for low-birth-weight infants is available from the WHO Guidelines on Optimal Feeding of Low Birth-Weight Infants in Lowand Middle-Income Countries. Infants and mothers living with HIV can refer to current guidelines on HIV and infant feeding. The guideline aims to assist WHO Member States and their partners in making evidence-informed decisions to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and implement the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Nutrition, the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030), and the Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding. The development of this guideline followed a systematic process, including identifying priority questions, retrieving evidence, assessing and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and impact evaluation. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology was used to prepare evidence profiles based on systematic reviews. The DECIDE framework was employed to guide the formulation of recommendations, considering intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The available evidence included 22 systematic reviews assessing the effects of interventions to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding in facilities providing maternity and newborn services. The quality of evidence varied from very low to high for critical outcomes such as breastfeeding rates, nutrition, and health. Additional qualitative evidence was synthesized to assess mothers' values and preferences regarding the benefits and harms of interventions and the acceptability of interventions to health workers. The findings were appraised using the GRADE-CERQual approach, which evaluates confidence in qualitative evidence based on methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. The guideline provides specific recommendations, such as facilitating early and uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact between mothers and infants, supporting mothers to initiate breastfeeding within the first hour after delivery, and providing practical support to manage breastfeeding difficulties. It also emphasizes the importance of rooming-in practices, responsive feeding, and discouraging the use of food or fluids other than breast milk unless medically indicated. For preterm infants unable to breastfeed directly, non-nutritive sucking and oral stimulation may be beneficial. Feeding methods such as cups or spoons are preferred over feeding bottles and teats for preterm infants when expressed breast milk or other feeds are medically indicated.
